value.title: Cross-model review r2 — claude-inbound-accept-global
value.note:
Round 2: adjudication of every r1 finding (f1-f8) against the current working tree, plus what the round-2 fixes introduced.

SUBJECT: still the WORKING TREE. Judged snapshot (git hash-object): claude_settings.rs 6d5b2dfd, cli/src/main.rs 87b42510, cli/tests/claude_inbound.rs 2a4723b0, daemon/src/registration.rs 6bf631f3 (UNCHANGED from r1 — see #findings/a3), daemon/src/http/identity.rs f69977ce.

METHOD, per packet i6: the PM's green claim was re-derived, not accepted. Targeted suites re-run and watched: pij-harnesses claude_settings 10/10, pij-daemon registration 1/1, pij-cli --test claude_inbound 2/2, pij-cli caller-warning unit 1/1 — 14/14, matching the PM's count exactly. Then, independently of those tests, I ran the real `pij-rs` binary by hand: two daemon boots against a temp HOME with a seeded keyless settings.json, and the doctor verb against four file states. Full workspace NOT re-run, per the dispatcher's instruction.

HEADLINE: all eight r1 findings are resolved — six fixed in code, two resolved by prime's rulings plus the code that implements them. One NEW MAJOR was introduced by the round-2 fixes themselves, and it is a direct interaction between two of them (#findings/n1). One round more.

AC RE-JUDGEMENT
- AC1 remains TRUE, and is now stronger: the shell half that carried the r1 caveat is fixed, and the empty-file case moved from refusal to repair under prime's ruling.
- AC2 flips to TRUE. The integration test the AC named now exists, and I re-derived its claim by hand rather than trusting it: two real boots produced exactly one `config.claude-inbound-ensured` row, with the log line reading `touched` then `skipped`.
- AC3 unchanged from r1 (TRUE, re-derived there from the native transcript and the isolated spine). Nothing in this round touches the delivery path.
- AC4 remains TRUE for the doctor's read-only behaviour, but the doctor's OUTPUT now has a correctness defect that AC4's 'output pasted for both homes' does not catch — see #findings/n1. Per the dispatcher's instruction the full workspace was not re-run this round, so the 'project gates green' half of AC4 rests on r1's run plus these 14 targeted tests.

WHAT I CHECKED FOR REGRESSION while confirming the fixes: LF-only documents still get LF separators (the CRLF fix did not invert); malformed documents (BOM, `//` comments, trailing comma) are still refused untouched; the duplicate-key last-wins behaviour still holds; 0600 file permissions survive the new atomic replace.

value.finding:
NEW, introduced by this round: the doctor now contradicts the writer about the exact file state prime just ruled on.

CLAIM: prime ruled that an empty or whitespace-only settings.json is MISSING, and `plan_inbound_accept` was changed accordingly (L85-90: `existing.trim().is_empty()` returns a Write). `inspect_claude_inbound` did not get that ruling. It reports such a file as `status: "error"`, `error: "malformed settings.json: EOF while parsing a value..."`.

PROOF, run against the built binary rather than reasoned about:
```
$ : > $HOME/settings.json
$ pij-rs --json doctor claude-inbound
{"home":"...","current":null,"required":"accept","status":"error",
 "error":"malformed settings.json: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 0"}
```
and the same for a whitespace-only file (`line 2 column 0`). Meanwhile the probe over the public planner returns `WRITE ... out={\n  "crossSessionInbound": "accept"\n}\n` for `""`, `"   \n"` and `"\t\t"` alike. So the diagnostic says 'malformed, pij will refuse to touch this' about a file pij will in fact back up and rewrite on its next boot.

WHY IT APPEARED NOW, which is the part worth fixing properly: in r1 the inspector CALLED the planner (`match plan_inbound_accept(Some(&existing))`), so the two surfaces could not disagree — a change to the classification propagated for free. The f5 fix rewrote `inspect_claude_inbound` to parse the document itself (L140-158), duplicating the classification. The f7 ruling then landed in the planner only. Two independently correct fixes, and the seam between them is where the defect lives: one file state now has two owners with two opinions.

This is the shape my r1 f4 and f5 rows were about, one layer along: a surface whose job is to REPORT the state is wired to different logic than the code that ACTS on it, so it lies exactly when consulted about the interesting case.

SMALLEST FIX: give the inspector the same empty-is-missing branch — `if existing.trim().is_empty()` yields `file_exists: true, current: None, error: None`, which the doctor already renders as `key-missing`. Better, and barely larger: have `inspect_claude_inbound` classify by calling `plan_inbound_accept` again, so the ruling has exactly one home. Add the empty-file case to the doctor's own test, which currently covers file-missing, key-missing and not-accept but not this one.
value.receipt: pij-rs --json doctor claude-inbound run against empty and whitespace-only files; probe over plan_inbound_accept for the same three inputs; r1 vs r2 inspect_claude_inbound compared directly

value.finding:
r1 f1 (non-atomic rewrite of the operator's live settings.json) — FIXED, verified.

`atomic_replace` (L238-266) creates `.settings.json.pij-<pid>-<seq>.tmp` with `create_new`, writes, `sync_all`s, copies the original file's permissions onto the temp, drops the handle and `fs::rename`s over the target; on any error it removes the temp. The truncation window is gone: the target path now moves from one complete document to another in a single rename.

VERIFIED BY HAND, not by the test: seeded a 0600 settings.json, ran two real daemon boots, and the file came back 0600 with the expected content and a timestamped backup beside it. The `TEMP_SEQUENCE` counter means two ensures inside one process cannot collide on the temp name.

TWO RESIDUALS, neither blocking, both stated so they are not mistaken for oversights:
(1) The read-modify-write RACE is still there — a change written by Claude Code between our read and our rename is still lost. I said in r1 that the rename removes the corruption mode and is the disproportionate share of the value, and I stand by that; a lock or compare-before-write is a bigger change and prime should decide whether it is wanted, not the reviewer.
(2) There is no directory fsync after the rename, so a crash immediately after can leave the directory entry pointing at the old file. That loses a repair, not data, and the next boot redoes it.
value.receipt: claude_settings.rs:238-266 read; two hand-run boots with a seeded 0600 file; ls -l before and after

value.finding:
r1 f2 (AC2 had no test) — FIXED, and independently re-derived.

`daemon_boot_repairs_once_and_publishes_one_change_event` boots the real `pij-rs` binary twice against one state dir with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`/`HOME` pointed at a temp home, waits for the actual `listening on` line, SIGINTs, and then queries the spine with sqlx: exactly 1 `config.claude-inbound-ensured` after the first boot, still exactly 1 after the second. This is the right shape — a real process, the real log line as the readiness signal, and a count assertion that cannot pass vacuously (a missing hook gives 0, a double publish gives 2). `boot_once` panics with captured stdout and stderr if readiness never arrives, so a silently-failing daemon cannot masquerade as a pass.

Because a regression test that has never been observed to fail is a claim rather than a witness, I did not rely on it. I ran the same experiment by hand with the built binary: two boots, temp home seeded with `{"theme":"dark"}`, and counted the rows myself:
```
boot 1: pij-rs claude inbound: <home>=touched
boot 2: pij-rs claude inbound: <home>=skipped
sqlite> select count(*) ... kind='config.claude-inbound-ensured'  ->  1
```
The payload was `{"after":"accept","before":null,"home":"<home>"}` and the resulting file was `{\n  "theme": "dark",\n  "crossSessionInbound": "accept"\n}`. AC2 is now true on evidence I generated.

`sqlx` was added to crates/cli under [dev-dependencies], not [dependencies] — checked, because a test-only dependency landing in the production section would be the easy mistake here.
value.receipt: cli/tests/claude_inbound.rs:44-142 read in full; test re-run (2/2); independent two-boot run with sqlite3 count; crates/cli/Cargo.toml section checked

value.finding:
r1 f3 (a config note that cannot be recorded prevented the daemon from starting) — FIXED, correctly and narrowly.

Both failure arms at the boot call site now warn and continue: a clock failure prints `Claude inbound setting changed but its config event timestamp failed` and `continue`s to the next report; a publish failure prints `... could not be published` and falls through. Neither shuts the daemon down, and the `listening on` line is still reached — which my two hand-run boots confirm end to end.

DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED, and I want this recorded rather than passed over: `registration.rs` is byte-identical to r1 (hash 6bf631f3), so the registration path still fails the registration when its publish fails (`map_err(RegistrationError::Runtime)?`). That is exactly the asymmetry my r1 verdict v3 asked for — at boot the failing operation is everything, at registration it is the caller's own operation and the caller is told. Correct as it stands; not an oversight.
value.receipt: cli/src/main.rs:880-930 read; registration.rs hash compared against the r1 snapshot; two hand-run boots reached listening on

value.finding:
r1 f4 (`EnsureReport.after` hardcoded to "accept" on the read-only path) — FIXED at the reported site.

The read-only path now returns a dedicated `ClaudeInboundState { home, file_exists, current, error }` with no `after` field at all, which is the better of the two fixes I suggested: the type can no longer express the false claim.

RESIDUAL, narrower than the r1 finding and reported as such: `EnsureReport.after` is still unconditionally `"accept"` (L279), including on refusal and error rows where nothing was written. Both consumers read it only inside a `report.changed` filter, so nothing renders it falsely today. It is latent, it is smaller than what I filed, and I am not asking for it this round — but the type is still public and the field name still invites the wrong read.
value.receipt: claude_settings.rs:41-47 and 270-284 read; both consumers (cli/src/main.rs, registration.rs) checked for reads outside the changed filter

value.finding:
r1 f5 (doctor conflated 'no settings.json' with 'file present, key absent') — FIXED.

`ClaudeInboundState.file_exists` now carries the distinction and the doctor's status ladder renders five states: `error`, `accept`, `not-accept`, `key-missing`, `file-missing`. The CLI integration test asserts `file-missing` and `key-missing` on a real binary invocation, and asserts the file is byte-identical afterwards, so read-only-ness is still proven by an assertion rather than by prose.

The fix is correct for the states it covers. It is also the direct cause of #findings/n1, because it made the doctor classify independently of the planner instead of through it — worth carrying that connection forward when n1 is fixed, so the two surfaces end up sharing one classifier rather than agreeing by coincidence.
value.receipt: cli/src/main.rs:872-905 read; cli/tests/claude_inbound.rs re-run (2/2); doctor run by hand against four file states

value.finding:
r1 f6 (interface drift; risk r2 unmitigated) — RESOLVED: half fixed, half ruled.

FIXED: `claude_homes_from` is now `pub` with a doc comment, which is the guide's stated interface. Confirmed by calling it from outside the repo: `claude_homes_from(Some("/tmp/x"), Some("/tmp")) -> ["/tmp/x"]`.

RULED: prime deferred the caller-supplied write target — no field on the registration claim — and asked instead for a read-only warning. `caller_claude_warning` (L823) delivers it: on `adopt` with harness Claude and a non-empty `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` whose settings do not read accept, it prints `caller CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR <path> does not set crossSessionInbound=accept; daemon registration writes only daemon-derived homes`. The second clause is the important one and it is accurate: it tells the operator the true limit rather than implying pij will handle it. It is genuinely read-only (it calls the inspector), and the unit test covers the warn case, the accept case and the non-Claude case.

TWO SMALL LIMITS, recorded not demanded: the warning is wired to the `adopt` arm only, so `pij register` gets nothing; and it fires even when the caller's `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` happens to BE a daemon-derived home that the very next registration will repair, which reads as a false alarm at that moment. Both are consistent with prime's deferral and neither misleads about the write behaviour.
value.receipt: cli/src/main.rs:816-840 read; unit test re-run (1/1); claude_homes_from called from an out-of-repo probe crate

value.finding:
r1 f7 (empty/whitespace settings.json refused as malformed) — RULED and IMPLEMENTED. This row closes the question I raised.

Prime ruled empty-or-whitespace is MISSING. `plan_inbound_accept` L85-90 returns the same fresh-document Write the absent-file branch returns, and because the file exists on disk `ensure_home` takes the backup branch first — so the operator's bytes, whatever they were, are copied to `settings.json.bak-<unix-ms>` before anything is written. Backup-first repair, as described.

Re-derived over all three forms rather than the one the test uses: `""`, `"   \n"` and `"\t\t"` each plan the same valid, idempotent document. `empty_and_whitespace_files_are_backed_up_then_repaired` covers it in-tree.

The ruling reached the writer but not the reader — that is #findings/n1, and it is filed there rather than here so this row can stay closed.
value.receipt: claude_settings.rs:85-90 and 178-200 read; probe over three empty forms; harness test re-run (10/10)

value.finding:
r1 f8 (LF-only line inserted into a CRLF document) — FIXED.

`insert_top_level_property` picks `line_break` from whether the document contains `
` (L337-341). Verified both directions from outside the repo, because a separator fix that inverts is the obvious way for this to go wrong:
- CRLF in -> `{
  "a": 1,
  "crossSessionInbound": "accept"
}
`
- LF in -> `{
  "a": 1,
  "crossSessionInbound": "accept"
}
` (unchanged behaviour, no regression)
Both valid and idempotent. `insertion_preserves_crlf_line_endings` covers it in-tree.

One unremarkable consequence: a document already mixing CRLF and LF gets a CRLF separator throughout. The input was already inconsistent; not a defect.
value.receipt: claude_settings.rs:332-358 read; probe rows crlf-insert, crlf-replace, lf-still-lf, mixed

value.finding:
The atomic replace preserves permissions, as claimed — and silently drops extended attributes and ACLs, which was not claimed either way.

MEASURED, since 'preserves permissions' and 'preserves file metadata' are different claims and only the first was made: seeded a settings.json at 0600 with a custom xattr, ran a real boot, and compared:
```
before: -rw-------@  ... com.apple.provenance, com.example.probe
after:  -rw-------@  ... com.apple.provenance
```
Mode survives (the r2 claim is true). `com.example.probe` is gone, because rename installs a NEW inode and only `permissions` is copied across; `com.apple.provenance` reappears only because macOS re-adds it. The operator's real `~/.claude/settings.json` carries the `@` flag today, so this path is live rather than hypothetical.

Low consequence — settings.json xattrs are normally provenance or quarantine marks, and the backup still holds the original inode. Filed so the limit is on the record rather than discovered later. Smallest fix if wanted: copy xattrs onto the temp before the rename; otherwise state the limit in the function's doc comment.
value.receipt: ls -l@ before and after a real boot with a seeded custom xattr

value.finding:
A stale temp file from a recycled pid costs one spurious error before it self-heals.

The temp name is `.settings.json.pij-<pid>-<seq>.tmp` and it is opened `create_new`. If a previous process died between create and rename, and the OS later hands the same pid to a new pij (pids reset at boot and are reused constantly on this machine), `create_new` fails and the ensure reports `could not write ... atomically: File exists`. It then self-heals, because the error arm removes the temp — so the NEXT boot or registration succeeds.

One noisy error, no data at risk, and the sequence counter already rules out same-process collisions. Recorded because 'it failed once and then worked' is a confusing thing to meet cold. Smallest fix if wanted: `OpenOptions::truncate` instead of `create_new`, or add the boot time to the temp name.
value.receipt: claude_settings.rs:239-266 read; create_new and the error-arm remove_file traced

value.finding: #findings/a1
value.rationale: r1 f1 fixed. Atomic temp+sync+rename with permissions carried over; verified on a real boot, not just in the test. Two residuals recorded (the read-modify-write race, no directory fsync) — both are prime's call on scope, not regressions.

value.finding: #findings/a2
value.rationale: r1 f2 fixed and AC2 flips to true. The test is well-shaped and non-vacuous, and I re-derived its claim with two hand-run boots rather than trusting a green I did not generate.

value.finding: #findings/a3
value.rationale: r1 f3 fixed at the boot site, and correctly NOT changed at the registration site — the asymmetry my r1 verdict asked for is exactly what shipped.

value.finding: #findings/a4
value.rationale: r1 f4 fixed by making the false claim inexpressible — a dedicated read-only type rather than a nulled-out field. Residual on EnsureReport.after is latent-only and explicitly not asked for this round.

value.finding: #findings/a5
value.rationale: r1 f5 fixed; five distinct statuses, asserted against the real binary. Note the causal link to n1 — the fix is correct and still created the seam.

value.finding: #findings/a6
value.rationale: r1 f6 resolved: the public resolver is the code half, prime's deferral is the ruling half, and the adopt warning states the true limit rather than papering over it. Prime ruled; I am not re-litigating scope.

value.finding: #findings/a7
value.rationale: r1 f7 was a question and prime answered it. Backup-first repair implemented and re-derived across all three empty forms. The unresolved half of the ruling lives in n1, not here.

value.finding: #findings/a8
value.rationale: r1 f8 fixed; checked in both directions so a separator fix that inverted would not pass as a fix.

value.finding: #findings/n1
value.rationale: NEW and the only thing standing between this branch and the PR. Proven against the built binary: the doctor calls an empty settings.json 'malformed' while the writer repairs it. It exists because f5 and f7 were fixed independently and the classification acquired two owners. Fix by giving the ruling one home — have the inspector classify through plan_inbound_accept — and add the empty-file case to the doctor test.

value.finding: #findings/n2
value.rationale: Measured, low consequence, not blocking. The round-2 claim ('preserving permissions') is TRUE as stated; this records the limit next to it so nobody later reads it as 'preserving file metadata'.

value.finding: #findings/n3
value.rationale: Self-healing, one spurious error, no data at risk. Recorded for the operator who meets it cold; fix is optional.
